title: Bass guitar
wiki_lead:
The bass guitar, also known as the electric bass (or simply bass), is the lowest-pitched member of the guitar family. It is similar in appearance and construction to an electric guitar but with a longer neck and scale length. The electric bass guitar most commonly has four strings, though five-, six-, seven-, eight- and twelve-stringed models are also built. The electric bass guitar was invented in the mid-1950s to replace the double bass in popular music due to its lighter weight, smaller size and easier portability, most models' inclusion of frets for easier intonation, and electromagnetic pickups for amplification. 
The electric bass guitar is usually tuned the same as the double bass, corresponding to pitches one octave lower than the four lowest-pitched strings of a guitar, typically E, A, D, and G (5-string models typically add a low B, and 6-string models typically add a high C). It is played with the fingers, thumb or with a pick. 
Because the electric bass guitar is a quiet instrument acoustically, it requires external amplification, generally via electromagnetic or piezo-electric pickups. It can also be used with direct input boxes, audio interfaces, mixing consoles, computers, or bass-effects processors which offer headphone jacks.

Terminology
The New Grove Dictionary of Music and Musicians refers to this instrument as an "Electric bass guitar, usually with four heavy strings tuned E1'–A1'–D2–G2." It also defines bass as "Bass (iv). A contraction of Double bass or Electric bass guitar." Mottola's Cyclopedic Dictionary of Lutherie Terms begins its definition of the instrument as "A bass guitar that produces sound primarily with the aid of electronic devices." According to some authors the proper term is "electric bass". Common names for the instrument are "bass guitar", "electric bass guitar", "electric bass", and simply "bass". and some authors claim that they are historically accurate. A bass guitar whose neck lacks frets is termed a fretless bass.


Scale

The scale of a bass is defined as the length of the vibrating strings between the nut and the bridge saddles. On a modern 4-string electric bass guitar, 30" (76 cm) or less is considered short scale, 32" (81 cm) medium scale, 34" (86 cm) standard scale and 35" (89 cm) long scale. Long scale is more commonly seen on 5-string basses and above to allow for better resonance of the low B string.
The double bass is "acoustically imperfect" like the viola. For a double bass to be acoustically perfect, its body size would have to be twice as that of a cello, rendering it practically unplayable, so the double bass is made smaller to make it playable. The pickups in an electric bass guitar addresses the compromises of a double bass by allowing the low notes to be amplified electronically.


Pickup

Pickups are attached to the body of the guitar beneath the strings. They are responsible for converting the vibrations of the strings into interference of a magnetic field which is converted into analogous electrical voltage sent as input to an instrument amplifier.


Strings

Bass guitar strings are composed of a core and winding. The core is a wire which runs through the center of the string and is made of steel, nickel, or an alloy. The winding is a smaller gauge wire wrapped around the core. Bass guitar strings vary by the material and cross-sectional shape of the winding. 
Common string variants include roundwound, flatwound, halfwound (groundwound), coated, tapewound and taperwound strings. Roundwound and flatwound strings feature windings with circular and rounded-square cross-sections, respectively, with half-round  strings being a hybrid between the two. Coated strings have their surface coated with a synthetic layer while tapewound strings feature a metal core with a plastic winding. grok_lead: The bass guitar, also known as the electric bass, is a stringed musical instrument that produces low-frequency tones, typically featuring four strings tuned an octave below a standard electric guitar to E1, A1, D2, and G2, and serves as the primary low-end instrument in rhythm sections across genres like rock, jazz, pop, and funk. It consists of a solid or semi-hollow body, a fretted or fretless neck, electromagnetic pickups for amplification, and is played by plucking or slapping the strings with the fingers or a pick, providing harmonic foundation and rhythmic drive essential to ensemble music. Unlike the upright double bass, which it largely replaced in modern bands due to its portability and louder output, the bass guitar enables precise intonation and easier playability in amplified settings. The instrument's origins trace back to the 1930s, when inventor Paul Tutmarc developed the first fretted, solid-body electric bass, the Audiovox Model 736, as a compact alternative to the cumbersome acoustic double bass used in jazz orchestras. Early prototypes faced challenges with amplification technology, limiting adoption until the post-World War II era, when improved pickups and amplifiers made electric instruments viable. The breakthrough came in 1951 with Leo Fender's introduction of the Precision Bass (P-Bass), the first mass-produced electric bass, featuring a slab body, split-coil pickup, and 34-inch scale length for enhanced low-end clarity and sustain. This model revolutionized music by allowing bassists like Monk Montgomery to perform amplified solos and walking lines in jazz, while its adoption in rock 'n' roll bands addressed the need for volume in larger venues. Subsequent innovations expanded the bass guitar's versatility and popularity. In 1956, the Hofner 500/1 "Beatle Bass" offered a lightweight, violin-shaped semi-hollow design, famously used by Paul McCartney to define the Beatles ' sound. Fender's 1960 Jazz Bass introduced a slimmer neck and brighter tone via single-coil pickups, influencing funk and fusion players, while the 1966 Ampeg AUB-1 marked the first commercial fretless model for smoother glissando effects. By the 1970s, five- and six-string variants emerged to access lower pitches like B0 without detuning, and active electronics added onboard preamps for tonal shaping. Today, bass guitars range from boutique custom builds to affordable student models, with materials like alder, ash, or maple bodies and nickel-plated steel strings standard for durability and resonance. In popular music, the bass guitar underpins groove and structure through techniques such as root-note patterns, syncopated rhythms, and melodic lines, collaborating closely with drums to form the backbone of tracks in styles from Motown soul to heavy metal. Iconic players like James Jamerson, Jaco Pastorius, and Flea have elevated it from accompaniment to lead instrument, incorporating slap-pop, tapping, and effects pedals to explore timbres beyond traditional pizzicato. Its enduring influence stems from enabling portable, high-volume performance, transforming ensemble dynamics since the mid-20th century.
